Lactantius
lak-TAN-shus
proper noun
From the Latin Lactantius, a Roman family name perhaps connected with lactans, “giving milk, nourishing.” His full name was Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius; he flourished about 250 to 325 and was surnamed by later ages “the Christian Cicero” for the elegance of his Latin prose.

📖 Biblical Definition

Lactantius was a Christian teacher of rhetoric in the age of the last great persecution and the dawn of Constantine’s peace, a man so polished in his Latin that later ages named him “the Christian Cicero.” Converted from paganism, he turned the eloquence he had once employed in the schools of the empire to the defence of the faith, setting forth in his great work, the Divine Institutes, a reasoned overthrow of the folly of idolatry and the wisdom of the philosophers, and a commendation of the true God and of the righteousness that comes by Him. He wrote also of the deaths of the persecutors, recounting how the LORD requited those emperors who had lifted their hands against His church, a solemn testimony that the God who is not mocked will render to every man according to his deeds. So esteemed was his learning that the emperor Constantine appointed him tutor to his son Crispus. Not every point of his doctrine is to be received without weighing, for his early training left traces of imperfection in his grasp of the deep things of God, and he wrote before the great creeds had refined the church’s speech; yet his labour to show that the wisdom of the world is foolishness with God, 1 Corinthians 3:19, and to commend the gospel to a learned and pagan age, marks him a faithful and useful witness whose eloquence was laid at the feet of Christ.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A Christian rhetorician surnamed the Christian Cicero, author of the Divine Institutes and tutor to Constantine’s son.

LACTANTIUS, proper noun. A Christian teacher of rhetoric flourishing about 250 to 325, in the age of Diocletian and Constantine.

Surnamed the Christian Cicero for the elegance of his Latin prose, converted from paganism to the faith.

Author of the Divine Institutes, a reasoned defence of the true God against idolatry and pagan philosophy.

Author also of a treatise on the deaths of the persecutors, recounting God’s judgment upon the enemies of His church.

Appointed by the emperor Constantine to be tutor to his son Crispus.

📖 Key Scripture

1Co 3:19 — "For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness."

1Co 1:27 — "But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty."

Psa 14:1 — "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, they have done abominable works, there is none that doeth good."

Gal 6:7 — "Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A faithful and eloquent apologist, not a contested doctrine; his life recovers the principle that all learning must serve the truth of God.

expand to see more

Lactantius took the eloquence he had learned in the pagan schools and consecrated it wholly to the defence of the faith, overthrowing the folly of idolatry and setting the true God before a learned and unbelieving age — a labour that shows how the church may plunder the treasures of the world’s learning and lay them at the feet of Christ.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle his life recovers is that all human learning, eloquence, and philosophy find their right use only in the service of the truth of God, and that the wisdom of this world, however polished, is foolishness with Him when it is set against His gospel. Though Lactantius wrote before the creeds had refined the church’s speech, and not every judgment of his is to be followed, his consecrated eloquence remains a pattern: gifts of mind are not to be despised but to be baptized into the service of Christ, that the wise of the world may be taken in their own craftiness and brought to bow before the wisdom of God.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

That the learning and eloquence of the world are rightly used only when laid at the feet of Christ.

God is not mocked; He requites the persecutors who lift their hands against His church.

Usage

"Lactantius, the Christian Cicero, laid his pagan eloquence at the feet of Christ in the Divine Institutes."

"His treatise on the deaths of the persecutors testifies that God is not mocked."

"Constantine esteemed his learning enough to make him tutor to his son Crispus."
